pathology: Categorical crowding-out — incentive/sanction reframes situation as transactional, destroying pre-existing moral norm
llm_evidence: Not isolated in LLM benchmarks; agents in GovSim/SanctSim lack intrinsic motivation that could be crowded out
key_references: Gneezy & Rustichini (2000) Haifa daycare; Bowles (2016) The Moral Economy; Frey & Jegen (2001)

pathology: Marginal crowding-out — increasing incentive magnitude reduces net compliance (norm erosion > direct incentive effect)
llm_evidence: Not tested. LLM agents respond to payoff magnitudes but lack norm internalization to erode.
key_references: Bowles & Polania-Reyes (2012) JPublicEcon; Cardenas et al. (2000) Colombian commons field experiments

pathology: Control aversion — punishment/monitoring signals distrust, reducing autonomous motivation of monitored party
llm_evidence: Partially: SanctSim tests punishment but doesn't measure whether cooperative disposition degrades due to being monitored
key_references: Falk & Kosfeld (2006) 'Hidden Costs of Control' AER; Ellingsen & Johannesson (2008) morale erosion

pathology: Frame-shifting — explicit incentive moves cognitive frame from ethical/communal to market/exchange
mechanisms_targeted: Payment for public goods, carbon taxes
llm_evidence: Not tested. LLM agents lack dual ethical/market frames in current architectures.
key_references: Titmuss (1970) blood donation; Bowles (2008); Ireland plastic bag tax as positive reframing example

pathology: Goodhart collapse — statistical regularity between proxy and goal breaks down under optimization pressure
mechanisms_targeted: Reputation scores, performance metrics, audit systems
llm_evidence: Highly relevant to LLM alignment: reward hacking and specification gaming are the ML analogue. Not tested in multi-agent governance benchmarks.
key_references: Goodhart (1975); Strathern (1997); Manheim & Garrabrant (2018) four failure modes

pathology: Campbell corruption — high-stakes use of quantitative indicator corrupts both indicator and social process
mechanisms_targeted: Achievement testing, publication metrics, KPI-driven management
llm_evidence: Not isolated. LLM evaluations are themselves subject to Campbell's law (benchmark saturation).
key_references: Campbell (1976); Muller (2018) The Tyranny of Metrics; teaching-to-the-test literature

pathology: Cobra effect — incentive designed to solve a problem creates new agents/strategies that worsen it
llm_evidence: Not tested in LLM multi-agent settings. Could be tested with adaptive agent populations.
key_references: Delhi cobra bounty; Hanoi rat bounty; hospital readmission gaming

pathology: Panoptic self-censorship — awareness of observation induces self-discipline beyond target behaviour
llm_evidence: Not tested. LLM agents don't model self-censorship or expressive behaviour distinct from strategic choice.
key_references: Foucault (1975) Discipline and Punish; Penney (2016) Wikipedia post-Snowden; Stoycheff et al. (2019)

pathology: Lateral surveillance / peer panopticon — peer-to-peer monitoring creates mutual distrust and conformity pressure
mechanisms_targeted: Gossip, peer punishment, social media visibility
llm_evidence: Partially: SanctSim implements peer sanctioning but doesn't measure trust degradation or over-conformity.
key_references: Andrejevic (2005) lateral surveillance; Marwick (2012) social media self-surveillance; Büchi et al. (2022)

pathology: Information avoidance — agents deliberately avoid feedback/transparency mechanisms to preserve self-image
mechanisms_targeted: Feedback systems, social comparison, transparency mandates
llm_evidence: Not tested in LLM benchmarks. Would require agents with self-image concerns.
key_references: Golman et al. (2017) 'Information Avoidance' JEL; Nikiforakis (2010) feedback avoidance in PGG

pathology: Antisocial punishment — punishment directed at high contributors rather than free-riders (spite, envy, norm disagreement)
llm_evidence: Partially: LLM agents in SanctSim can technically engage in antisocial punishment but not isolated as phenomenon.
key_references: Herrmann, Thöni & Gächter (2008) Science; Rand & Nowak (2011)

pathology: Power abuse / punisher entitlement — agents with punishment authority exploit it for gain or contribute less themselves
llm_evidence: Not tested. Relevant to AI governance: who monitors the monitor?
key_references: Kirchkamp & Mill (2020); Hoeft & Mill (2017) entitlement effects; Fehr & Rockenbach (2003)

pathology: Punishment dependency / institutional fragility — cooperation collapses immediately when punishment is removed
llm_evidence: Not tested with LLM agents, but highly relevant: do AI agents internalize norms or just respond to payoff structures?
key_references: Mekvabishvili et al. (2023); Gürerk et al. (2006) institutional choice; Galbiati & Vertova (2014)

pathology: Exclusion → inequality spiral — excluded agents lose resources, making future cooperation harder (poverty traps)
llm_evidence: Not tested. GovSim exclusion is permanent (resource depletion); re-entry dynamics unexplored.
key_references: Cinyabuguma et al. (2005); Maier-Rigaud et al. (2010) exclusion and inequality in PGG

pathology: Revenge cycles / feuds — punishment triggers counter-punishment, escalating conflict rather than restoring cooperation
